meta.citation: William Lilly, Christian Astrology (London, 1647), Wellcome Library copy, archive.org b30338724, Public Domain Mark. Page = printed page number.
meta.method: Every table cell transcribed from the page image (zoomed crops), not from OCR. Planet glyphs read by eye; where a glyph is damaged the reading and the cross-check are given in notes.

sources.quote: A Table of the Essentiall Dignities of the Planets according to Ptolomy
if you find a Planet in any of those Signes we call his house or houses, he is then essentially strong, and we allow for that five dignities
If he be in that Signe wherein he is exalted, you may allow him four dignities essentiall, whether he be neer the very degree of his exaltation, yea or not
If he be in any of those Signes which are alotted him for his Triplicity, he hath allowed him three dignities
If any Planet be in those degrees we assigne for his Termes, we allow him two dignities
he is then allowed one essentiall dignity; for being in his owne Decanate or Face, cannot then be called peregrine

essential.columns: Signs | Houses of the Planets (planet + D diurnal / N nocturnal) | Exaltation (planet + degree) | Triplicity of Planets (Di. / Noc.) | The Termes of the Planets (five cells: planet + end degree) | The faces of the Planets (three cells: planet + end degree) | Detriment | Fall
essential.scores_source: House 5, exaltation 4, triplicity 3, term 2, face 1 from the printed text pp.101-103 (quoted above). Detriment -5 and fall -4 from the printed p.115 table ('In his Detriment 5', 'In his Fall 4', listed under Debilities). The bottom row of the p.104 table in this copy carries figures 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 4 that are written in ink by hand (not printed type); the mark under 'Houses of the Planets' is an illegible handwritten figure (reads like o'). They agree with the printed text but are not used as the source.
essential.reading: Each printed cell is 'glyph number' (planet first, then the number); the term and face numbers are END degrees (Lilly p.105: 'the first six degrees of Aries are the Termes of Jupiter; from six to fourteen, the Termes of Venus'). A planet at 6°00' of Aries is in the second term (Venus): engine uses start < longitude-in-sign <= end, i.e. degree 0-6 = first term.
notes: No cell of the printed table was found to contradict Lilly's own planet chapters (term lists pp.57, 62, 65-66, 73, 76-77; exaltations and falls pp.57, 62, 65, 69, 73, 76, 80). No misprint is recorded.

Cancer and Leo: the Houses column prints both letters 'N' over 'D' beside the Moon and the Sun (each luminary has one house, p.104 'except Sol and Luna, they but one apiece'). Recorded as house_kind 'N D' as printed.

Leo, third term (end 19): the glyph has a dot above the circle and no visible horns; read as Venus. Cross-check: Venus' terms in Leo are 'In Leo, 14 15 16 17 18 19' (p.73), and Leo's second term (end 13) is a clear Mercury.
Sagittarius, second term (end 14): glyph faint; read as Venus. Cross-check: Venus' terms in Sagittarius are '9 10 11 12 13 14' (p.73); the third term (end 19) is a clear Mercury.
Pisces, triplicity night cell: the Mars glyph is partly blotted with ink but legible as Mars (text p.105: Mars rules the watery triplicity day and night).

Gemini exaltation and Sagittarius exaltation print the Dragon's Head and the Dragon's Tail respectively (text under the table: the Dragon's Head in 3 Gemini); the Gemini fall cell prints the Tail and the Sagittarius fall cell the Head. Both fall glyphs are damaged; the reading follows the exaltations. Lilly's p.115 table scores no dignity for the nodes, and nodes are not planets (p.25), so the engine does not score node dignity.
Exaltation degrees are informational: Lilly allows the 4 points anywhere in the sign (p.102, quoted in sources).

Triplicity: day ruler counts only in a day figure and night ruler only in a night figure (p.102: the Sun in Aries by night gets 4 for exaltation but nothing for triplicity), Mars excepted, who rules the watery triplicity day and night.

sources.quote: here I will againe insert the Table of the quantity of their Orbs, although I have in the Planets severall descriptions mentioned them
they stand thus as I have found by the best Authors and my owne Experience

orbs.image_only_text: p.107, set in a narrow column beside the table (OCR scrambles it, so it is transcribed from the image and not used as a checked quote): 'I somtimes use the one, and sometimes the other, as my Memory best Remembereth them, and this without error.'

p107_table.columns: planet | Lilly's value (deg, min) | qualifier as printed | the other value (deg, min)
p107_table.header_note: The table is printed on p.107 under 'they stand thus as I have found by the best Authors and my owne Experience'; the left column is the one he prints first (deg, min) and the right column is introduced by the italic qualifiers. A brace joins the right column to the sentence 'I somtimes use the one, and sometimes the other'.

Saturn.quote: His Orbe is nine degrees before and after

Jupiter.quote: His Radiation or Orbe, is nine degrees before and after any of his aspect

Mars.quote: is onely seven degrees before and after any of his aspects

Sun.quote: Is 15. degrees before any aspect; and so many after separations

Venus.quote: Her Orbe is 7. before and after any aspect of hers

Mercury.quote: His Orbe is seven degrees before and after any aspect

Moon.quote: Is 12. degrees before and after any Aspect

use.moiety_rule: Each planet is allowed half its own orb plus half the other planet's orb; two planets are within aspect (platic) while the distance from the exact aspect is less than the sum of the two moieties, and fully separated when that sum is exceeded.

sources.quote: for every Planet that applies is allowed halfe his owne orbs and halfe the orbs of that Planet from whom he separates
because she is within the moiety of both their Orbs; for the moity of Saturn his Rayes or Orbs is five
his influence begins to work, when either he applies, or any Planet applies to him, and is within nine degrees of his aspect

worked_examples_in_text: p.107: Venus 10 Taurus, Saturn 18 Virgo: moieties Saturn 5 + Venus 4 = 9 > 8 degrees from the exact trine, so platic trine (uses the left column: Saturn 10, Venus 8).

p.110: Jupiter separating from Saturn is clear of his rays only at 9 whole degrees: half of Jupiter's orb 4.30 + half of Saturn's 4.30 (uses Saturn 9 and Jupiter 9, the right column / planet chapters).
p.110: the Moon is separated from the Sun at 13.30 = half the Sun's orb 7.30 + 6 the moiety of her own (uses Sun 15 and Moon 12, the right column / planet chapters).

notes: Lilly's own figures disagree: the p.107 table's first column (Saturn 10, Jupiter 12, Mars 7.30, Sun 17, Venus 8, Mercury 7, Moon 12.30), the planet chapters (9, 9, 7, 15, 7, 7, 12), and the p.110 worked examples (Saturn 9, Jupiter 9, Sun 15, Moon 12) do not use one set. He says he uses either 'without error'.
The p.113 combustion rule (8.30 = 'the moyity of his owne Orbs', i.e. half of the Sun's 17) uses the p.107 first-column Sun value, while the p.110 example uses half of 15 for the Sun.
Mars, p.107: the qualifier printed is 'All consent' although the two columns differ (7.30 vs 7.0); recorded as printed.

The planet-chapter orbs are 'before and after' the aspect (a full orb, not a moiety), but the separation passage p.110 halves them. Whether the chapter wording means the full orb around each planet regardless of the other planet is left open by the text.

sources.quote: his middle motion is two minutes and one second

Saturn.quote: his middle motion is two minutes and one second; his diurnall motion sometimes is three, four, five, or six minutes, seldome more

Jupiter.quote: his midle motion is 4 min. 59 seconds: his Diurnall motion is 8 10 12, or 14 min. hardly any more

Mars.quote: His mean motion is 31 degr. 27 min.

Sun.quote: His meane motion is 59 8; yet his diurnall motion is sometimes 57m 16 seconds

Venus.quote: her meane motion is 59. min. and 8. seconds

Mercury.quote: his mean motion is 59. min. and 8. seconds; but he is sometimes so swift that he moveth one degree and 40. min. in a day, never more

Moon.quote: her meane motion is 13 degr. 10 min, and 36 seconds, but she moveth sometimes lesse and sometimes more, never exceeding 15 degr. and two min.

notes: Mars p.65 (image checked): printed 'His mean motion is 31 degr. 27 min.' immediately followed by 'His diurnall motion is sometimes 32 34 36 38 40 42 44 min. a day'. A mean motion of 31 degrees a day is impossible beside a diurnal motion of 32-44 minutes; suspected misprint for 31 min. 27 sec. The engine value [0,31,27] is this reading; the printed text is kept in 'printed'.

Sun p.69 (image checked): the maximum diurnal motion is blotted by ink in this copy ('never exceeding [blot] minutes and [blot] seconds'); a hand-written marginal note reads like '59:60'. Illegible; not used.
Lilly does not say in Book I that 'swift' means faster than this mean motion; see lilly.motion.swift_slow (operationalised).

sources.quote: When he moves not at all, as the superiours doe not 2,3, or 4, dayes before Retrogradation

Saturn.quote: He continueth Retrograde 140 dayes. He is five dayes in his first station before Retrogradation, and so many in his second station before Direction

Jupiter.quote: He is Retrograde about 120 dayes, is five dayes in his first station before retrogradation, and four dayes stationary before Direction

Mars.quote: he is retrograde 80 dayes; stationary before he be retrograde, two or three dayes

Venus.quote: she is two dayes stationary before retrogradation, and so many before direction , and doth usually continue retrograde 42 dayes

Mercury.quote: he is Stationary one day, and retrograde 24. dayes

Sun.quote: is alwayes direct, and never can be said to be Retrograde

Moon.quote: She is never Retrograde, but alwayes direct

notes: These are Lilly's round figures; the engine computes stations from the ephemeris (speed sign change) and uses these only for description.

sources.quote: he is not distant from the Sun eight degrees and thirty minutes, either before or after the Sun
untill he is fully elongated or distant from his body 17,degr. either before or after him
when he is not removed from him 17.min.or is within 17.min.forward or backward

notes: Combustion: 'in the same Signe where the Sun is' and within 8°30' (p.113); 'Combustion can onely be by personall conjunction in one Signe, not by any aspect' (p.114).

Under the sunbeams: 17 degrees 'either before or after him' (p.113). Lilly does not say whether the same sign is required nor whether the 8°30'-17° band excludes the combust zone; the p.115 table scores 'Combust' (-5) and 'Under the Sun Beames' (-4) as separate lines. Engine choice in lilly.sun.under_beams.
Cazimi: within 17 minutes 'forward or backward' (p.113); scored +5 'In the heart of the Sun, or Cazimi' (p.115). Lilly's example: Sun 15.30, planet 15.25 of the same sign.

sources.quote: A ready Table whereby to examine the Fortitudes and Debilities of the Planets
I forbear here to explaine the Table, because I shall doe it better hereafter upon some Example

rows.label_en: A Planet in his owne house, or in mutuall reception with another Planet by house, shall have Dignities
In his exaltation, or reception by exaltation
In the seventh, fourth and eleventh houses
Direct (the Sun and Moon are alwayes so, as to them this is voyd)
The Moon encreasing, or when she is Occidentall
Free from Combustion and Sun Beams
In the heart of the Sun, or Cazimi
In partill conjunction with Jupiter and Venus
In partill conjunction with the Dragon's Head
In partill trine to Jupiter and Venus
In partill sextile to Jupiter and Venus
In conjunction with Cor Leonis, in 24 degr. Leo
Or in conjunction with Spica Virginis, in 18 Libra
Partill conjunction with Saturn or Mars
Partill conjunction with the Dragon's Tail
Partill opposition of Saturn or Mars
Partill square of Saturn or Mars
In conjunction with Caput Algol in 20 Taurus, or within five degrees

fortitudes.reading: Printed as two columns: 'Essentiall Dignities' with 'Debilities' beside them, and 'Accidentall Fortitudes' with the accidental debilities beside them (that column has no printed heading). The debility numbers are printed without a minus sign; they are recorded here as negative because they stand under 'Debilities'. Planet and aspect glyphs read from the image (zoomed); labels expanded from glyphs to words (e.g. the conjunction glyph = 'conjunction').
notes: Misprints as printed (image checked): 'Caput Algot' (OCR 'Alget') for Caput Algol; 'Partill [conjunction] with [Saturn] r [Mars]' with the 'o' of 'or' missing; 'Partill [conjunction] wi h [Tail]' with the 't' missing; 'Partill [square] of [Saturn] er [Mars]' for 'or'. Meanings are clear; labels above are given in normal spelling.
Houses: all twelve houses are scored (10/1 +5; 7/4/11 +4; 2/5 +3; 9 +2; 3 +1; 12 -5; 8/6 -2). This order differs from the p.48 ranking (see house_strength).

The 'within five degrees' brace stands only against the Caput Algol line; Lilly gives no distance for Cor Leonis and Spica. The star positions are Lilly's 1647 longitudes (Regulus 24 Leo, Spica 18 Libra, Algol 20 Taurus); precession since then (about 5 degrees) is an engine question (see lilly.dignity.fixed_stars).

'With Jupiter and Venus' / 'of Saturn or Mars': the table is ambiguous whether 'and' means either planet or both; engine scores each partile contact with either planet (one line per contact) — see lilly.dignity.fortitude_table.
Lilly defers the use of the table to his examples (p.116) and does not say whether the totals are compared or how essential and accidental points combine.

sources.quote: To find out what Planet ruleth every hour of the Day or Night by the preceding Table
and the first hour of every day we assigne to that Planet assigned for the day, beginning at Sun-rise ever
for all that space of time which is contained from Sun rise to Sun-set, they divide into twelve equall parts
so that your Astrologicall hours are called unequall hours
We call Saturday his day, for then he begins to rule at Sun rise, and ruleth the first hour and eighth of that day
the length of the Planetary hour you must know by the rising of the Sun, and a Table hereafter following

rules: The planetary day runs from sunrise to the next sunrise (24 planetary hours), not from midnight or noon (p.482).
Sunrise to sunset is divided into 12 equal day hours; sunset to the next sunrise into 12 equal night hours: 'unequall hours', each 60 minutes only when the Sun enters Aries or Libra (pp.482-483).

The first hour after sunrise belongs to the day's planet; each following hour to the next planet in the order Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, continuing through the night (p.482, image checked: Sunday: Sun 1st, Venus 2nd, Mercury 3rd, Moon 4th, Saturn 5th, Jupiter 6th; this continued count gives the Moon the first hour on Monday, then Saturn, Jupiter, Mars).
Hence each day's planet also rules the 8th hour of its day (pp.61, 65, 68, 72, 76, 80, 83).
planetary_hours.table_location: Book II end: 'A Table whereby to find the Planetary hour' (contents p.20 lists it at p.474; the first table page with legible text is p.475 in this scan), followed by Chap. XCVII on its use, pp.482-483. Lilly's table gives sunrise times by the Sun's sign and degree for his latitude; the engine computes sunrise and sunset astronomically for the querent's place instead (operationalised, see lilly.method.planetary_hours).
planetary_hours.chaldean_order_source: Order named on p.482 ('seven Planets, viz. Saturne, Jupiter, Mars, Sol, Venus, Mercury, Luna') and confirmed by the hour sequence printed for Sunday (image checked).

sources.quote: the Succedants are next in vertue, the Cadents poore, and of little efficacy
in vertue is equivalent either to the seventh or fourth Houses
In the Mid-heaven or Ascendant

notes: p.48 order checked on the image: '1 10 7 4 11 5 9 3 2 8' with '6 12' at the line end (the last two numbers read from OCR and the page image at lower zoom).

Lilly's two rankings disagree: p.48 puts the 9th and 3rd (cadent) above the 2nd and 8th (succedent), though the same paragraph says succedents are next in virtue after angles; p.115 scores the 2nd (+3) above the 9th (+2) and the 3rd (+1), and gives the 1st and 10th equal points although p.48 ranks the 1st above the 10th.
The 6th is said to be unfortunate 'as having no aspect to the Ascendant' (p.54).
